title: The article and the Word
body_md:
Greek marks "the" with a little word called the article, which changes shape to match its noun. The most common forms are ὁ (masculine), ἡ (feminine), and τό (neuter). There is no separate word for "a/an" — a noun with no article is simply indefinite.

Our very first noun is λόγος, "word," which is masculine, so it takes ὁ: ὁ λόγος = "the word." Learn to spot the article — it is everywhere, and it tells you a noun is coming and often what role it plays.

Open the reading below and tap each word to reveal its meaning. You are already reading the New Testament.

readings.note: Find ὁ λόγος, 'the Word.' Notice the article ὁ before it.

exercises.prompt: Which article goes with the masculine noun θεός?

title: Saying "is" and "was" (εἰμί)
body_md:
The verb "to be" is the most common verb of all. You need just two forms to start reading:

ἐστιν — "is" (present)
ἦν — "was" (past)

Greek often drops the pronoun, because the verb ending already shows the person. And in a sentence like "God is light," the linking verb ἐστιν simply joins the subject (in the nominative case) to what is said about it.

readings.note: ἦν appears three times — 'was.' The Word 'was' in the beginning.
ὁ θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν — 'God is light.' ἐστιν links God to light.

title: Who does what: subject and object
body_md:
Greek shows a word's job by its ending (its case), not by word order. Two cases carry most of the load early on:

• the nominative marks the subject (the doer): ὁ λόγος
• the accusative marks the direct object (the receiver): τὸν λόγον

Notice the article changes too: ὁ (subject) → τόν (object). Because endings carry the meaning, Greek can put words in an order that would surprise an English reader — watch the endings, not the position.

readings.note: ὁ κόσμος (subject) and τὸν κόσμον / αὐτόν (object) — the same idea in two cases.

exercises.prompt: Is ὁ λόγος the subject or the object form?
How does 'the' change from subject to object for a masculine noun?

title: Joining ideas: καί, δέ, γάρ
body_md:
Little connecting words hold Greek sentences together, and they are extremely frequent:

καί — "and, also, even"
δέ — "but, and" (a gentle 'next'; it comes second in its clause)
γάρ — "for, because" (also comes second)

Spotting these instantly lets you see where one thought ends and the next begins.

readings.note: Three clauses joined by καί. The Word was with God, and the Word was God.

exercises.prompt: Where in its clause does δέ usually stand?

title: Present verbs: actions now
body_md:
A present-tense verb describes ongoing or general action. The endings show who is acting, so a single word can be a whole sentence: λέγει = "he says."

Start with a few very common verbs and their 3rd-person form (-ει, 'he/she/it …'):
λέγει (says), ἔχει (has), γινώσκει (knows), ἀγαπᾷ (loves).

readings.note: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς — 'Jesus says to him.' Find the verb λέγει.

exercises.prompt: What ending marks 'he/she/it' on a present verb here?

title: First-declension nouns: ἀγάπη and ζωή
body_md: Many feminine nouns end in -η in the nominative and take the article ἡ: ἡ ἀγάπη (love), ἡ ζωή (life). In a "X is Y" sentence the linking verb may be left unwritten or placed anywhere — the nominative endings tell you what is being equated.

readings.note: ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν — 'God is love.'
ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν — 'in him was life.'

exercises.prompt: Which article goes with the feminine noun ζωή?

title: Prepositions and their cases
body_md:
A preposition governs a noun in a particular case, and that pairing is part of the meaning. Three of the most common:

ἐν + dative — "in": ἐν ἀρχῇ (in the beginning)
εἰς + accusative — "into, to"
ἐκ + genitive — "out of, from"

Learn each preposition together with the case it takes.

readings.note: ἐν ἀρχῇ — 'in the beginning.' ἐν takes the dative ἀρχῇ.

title: Pronouns: αὐτός, ἐγώ, σύ
body_md:
Pronouns stand in for nouns and, like nouns, change by case. The workhorse is αὐτός ("he/it," and in other cases "him, his, to him"): αὐτῷ = "to/for him," αὐτόν = "him."

The first- and second-person pronouns are ἐγώ ("I") and σύ ("you"). They are often added for emphasis, since the verb ending already names the person.

readings.note: ἐν αὐτῷ — 'in him.' αὐτῷ is the dative of αὐτός.
ἐγώ εἰμι — 'I am.' Here ἐγώ is added for emphasis.

title: Adjectives that agree
body_md:
An adjective matches its noun in gender, number, and case. When an adjective sits between the article and the noun (or repeats the article), it is describing that noun: τὸν υἱὸν τὸν μονογενῆ = "the only son."

Agreement is your friend: matching endings link words that belong together, even when other words come between them.

readings.note: τὸν υἱὸν τὸν μονογενῆ — 'the only Son.' The adjective agrees with υἱόν.

exercises.prompt: In gender, number, and case, what must an adjective match?

title: The imperfect: the continuing past
body_md:
The imperfect tense describes past action seen as ongoing or repeated — "was doing, kept doing." You have already met one imperfect many times: ἦν, "was."

Most imperfects add an ε- at the front (the augment) and use past endings, e.g. ἠγάπα, "he was loving / used to love." For now, simply recognize ἦν and the augmented shape as signals of past time.

readings.note: ἦν — 'was.' The imperfect frames the Word as already existing.
ζωὴ ἦν — 'life was' (in him). Again the ongoing past.

exercises.prompt: What does the imperfect tense stress about a past action?
exercises.answer: that it was ongoing or repeated

title: The aorist: a past event as a whole
body_md:
The aorist tense reports a past action simply, as a single event: "it happened." A very common aorist is ἐγένετο, "came to be, happened, became."

Contrast it with the imperfect ἦν ("was, ongoing"): in John 1:14 the Word ἐγένετο flesh — a decisive event, not a state.

readings.note: ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο — 'the Word became flesh.' A single, decisive event (aorist).

exercises.prompt: How does the aorist view a past action, compared with the imperfect?
exercises.answer: as a single whole event, not as ongoing

title: Putting it together: reading John 3:16
body_md:
You now know enough to read one of the best-loved verses in the New Testament. Watch for what you have learned:

• the article and agreement: τὸν υἱὸν τὸν μονογενῆ
• a verb of action: ἠγάπησεν (he loved — an aorist of ἀγαπάω)
• the adjective αἰώνιον agreeing with ζωήν (eternal life)
• the little connectors and pronouns tying it together

Take it slowly, tap each word, and let the endings guide you. This is the goal of everything so far: reading the real text.

readings.note: Read it whole. οὕτως ('so') … ἠγάπησεν ('loved') … ζωὴν αἰώνιον ('eternal life').

exercises.prompt: ἠγάπησεν is a past-event (aorist) form of which verb?
